correctness.rationale: For n>=3, each noncontaining configuration has one angular gap greater than pi and a unique complementary semicircle anchor. Antipodal symmetry makes each semicircle mass 1/2, so the anchor has density f and the gap-deficit survival is exactly (1-2 integral f)^(n-1). The chord between extreme samples supports the hull and has center distance (r(theta)/2)*delta+O(delta^2), uniformly. Positive density gives a uniform exponential deficit tail, ensuring convergence of every fixed positive moment. Cauchy-Schwarz/Jensen proves unique density f proportional to r and convex-order dominance. The standalone checker independently reproduces sampled Cartesian hull distances and the exact circle CDF; no numerical run replaces the proof.

originality.rationale: The prior 1962 Wendel theorem establishes zero-versus-positive center exclusion but gives no marked clearance law; the 2014 Liu--Yang paper gives nonzero clearance for points uniformly inside the Euclidean disk, which is a different sampling model, and does not establish sampling-density independence or optimality on arbitrary symmetric smooth ovals. The other inspected 2023 extension concerns noncontainment under discrete-coordinate models. Queries of the public published-finding corpus finding index, geometry literature and the accessible historical random-polygon records yielded no dominating statement. Priority remains provisional.
residual_risks: Historical priority is provisional; the same metric result may exist under a different name such as halfspace-separation margin.
No full-text comparison was made with every related stochastic-geometry publication; references beyond the key two primary papers were inspected only to the reported extent.
The finite checker cannot independently certify all asymptotic uniformity statements, which rely on the analytic proof.

source_inspections.title: On the probability that the convex hull of random points contains the origin

value.rationale: Classical Wendel theory asks whether the center is missed; the natural next geometric invariant is the *metric extent* of that rare miss. The theorem gives a complete marked conditional limit for an entire class of smooth symmetric ovals, a new shape-dependent mixture rather than a point probability, a density-independent first moment, and a canonical sampling law uniquely minimizing every convex risk of the limit. This solves a motivated distribution-and-optimization problem with nontrivial geometric content beyond the circle order-statistic calibration.
